en: Postscript to the *Yimou Chao* (Excerpts on Bequeathing Plans), a Commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
This work was compiled by the Song dynasty master Yuanshi of Gushan, who annotated his own commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.

This book investigates the essence and reveals the subtle, causing the intent of the sutra and its commentary to become even more manifest; it is truly beneficial to all beings. However, the commentary has long been...

Although this commentary exists, it has not yet circulated; scholars have long regretted this. Recently, our Venerable Master In-gong (In’gong) examined and corrected it, and further added punctuation and annotations.
When I requested that he carve it into printing blocks, he asked me for a postscript.
Though my writing is not refined, I rejoiced in its completion and thus inscribed these humble words.
Written respectfully by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhikong in the fifth month of the Ji-hai year of the Hiobō era (1719), this is the *Commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra:
Bequeathing Counsel*. Preface: The principles of this scripture are profound and its phrasing essential.
In the past, the Master Zhongyong once provided a commentary based on the meaning of the "Three Contemplations. Fearing that my own ignorance might [misrepresent them], I have here...
Later generations were confused by the words of the *Shu* (Commentary), whereupon [the author] composed a *Chao* (Excerpts) to assist it, titled *Yimou* (Bequeathed Strategy).

He divided the *Shu* into two parts: first, the title; second, the main text. First, regarding the title: the main title is still concise, taking only four characters as the specific title for the *Shu*.
"Commentary" (*shu*) means to explain and clarify the meaning of the Sūtra. "Together with the Preface" (*bing xu*) indicates that there is a preface within the commentary.
Furthermore, the second [point] clarifies the location where the author resided: Mount Gu (Gushan).

Situated to the northwest of two lakes in Qiantang, it stands isolated and detached amidst the water, not connected to the surrounding mountains; thus, the world calls it "Mount Gu. [The author was a] śramaṇa.
The term "Śākya" (Shi) is a śramaṇa’s designation for the cessation of evil; "Śākya" in its full form is Śākyamuni, which translates as "Able One" (Nengren), his clan name.

There were non-Buddhists who also bore the title of śramaṇa, so they used "Śākya" to distinguish themselves from them. Furthermore, there were members of the Śākya clan who did not leave the household life, so they used "śramaṇa" to distinguish themselves from those laymen.
This is the purpose of using both terms together. Moreover, in ancient times in this land [of China], people all followed their teacher's surname.
For instance, Zhi Dun’s original surname was Guan; having left the household life under Zhi Falin, he consequently adopted the surname Zhi.
Dao’an once remarked that since those who have followed the Buddha to leave the household life ought to share the Buddha’s surname, from then on all śramaṇas referred to themselves as Śākya.

Furthermore, when the *Āgama* scriptures later arrived, it was indeed found that the four rivers, upon entering the sea, no longer retain their original names; likewise, those of the four castes who leave the household life become one.
To accord with the teachings of the Śākya clan, he was known as Zhidao (Wisdom Peace). His profound realization harmonized with the sacred scriptures, and his wisdom was perfect;

thus "Zhidao" was his name. His courtesy name was Wuwai (Boundless), and it is unknown where he was from. Having retired to Guishan to tend to his illness, he used that mountain to designate his place of residence.

His secular surname was Xu, and he styled himself Zhongyongzi (Master of the Doctrine of the Mean). He composed three chapters of the *Zhongyongzi zhuan* to express his intent, often lamenting this scripture.
The meaning of the Three Contemplations is such that the Way appears obscure; thus, people of later generations recite these words daily yet do not understand them.
Consequently, I have composed this commentary in a single day, saying: "I hope that in future generations there may arise those as enlightened as Zhiyi and Zhāng'ān.
If they were to comment upon it, my words would surely be reduced to ashes. That I now undertake this narration is simply because it cannot be avoided. How could I [otherwise]?"
How excellent is this name! It is like a person created by illusion who composes a commentary on illusion to instruct a crowd of illusory beings in their cultivation and study;

I cannot find its correctness, nor can I judge its high or low merit. This was on the eleventh day of the ninth month of autumn in the first year of the Tianxi era of the Great Song, the year of Ding-si.
The commentator says: "Zheng Kangcheng" refers to the one who expounds its meaning. The *Yueji* (Record of Music) states: "He who knows the rites..."
Those who possess the essence of joy can create; those who recognize the patterns of ritual and music can transmit them.

There are two original texts and two sections. First, the general preface. Second, the detailed explanation of the purpose and intent of the teachings. First, clarifying that written characters can manifest [the truth].

First, the direct clarification of the ultimate Way, which refers to the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*) and the *prajñā* of the true reality of ultimate emptiness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-prajñā*).
The name refers to the Prajñā of words and letters. Although principle and wisdom are identical and originally devoid of names or explanations, sentient beings do not realize this;

therefore, one must establish names to provide exposition and employ provisional verbal expressions to bring about cognitive understanding. Thus, words and letters are able to explain both [principle and wisdom].

Second, the conclusion derived from the preceding section shows that it originates from oneself. Because of non-awakening, one uses the name "prajñā" to designate the contemplation that is itself nameless;
and through explanations, whether extensive or concise, one speaks of the true mark (*dharmatā*) that is itself beyond speech.

Second, showing that the extensive and concise versions are adapted to different capacities. This section has two parts: first, the general introduction to the extensive and concise versions; second, clarifying that the principles of the extensive and concise versions are equal.

Regarding the first point—clarifying that the differences in the teachings arise from the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of those to be trained (*yogya*)—this refers to "capacity" (*yogya*) in terms of attaining awakening:

those with sharp faculties awaken upon hearing a brief exposition, whereas those with dull faculties require an extensive exposition before they can understand. If, however, "capacity" is defined in terms of retaining what is heard, then it refers to sharp faculties.
The ability to uphold the extensive version pertains to those of dull faculties who can only uphold the concise; this is not the intended meaning here. Regarding "extensive" and "concise":
"extensive" refers to the six hundred fascicles, while "concise" refers to fourteen lines. "Extensive" means a detailed exposition, which is also synonymous with "broad."
The second analogy below uses metaphors to reveal the underlying principle: the "fishing trap and snare" metaphor illustrates the extensive and concise teachings;

the "fish and rabbit" metaphor illustrates the principle of true emptiness. Zhuangzi said: "The fishing trap exists for the sake of the fish; once the fish is caught, one forgets the trap. The snare exists for the sake of the rabbit;
once the rabbit is caught, one forgets the snare. Words exist for the sake of the meaning; once the meaning is grasped, one forgets the words. The commentary states:
*Quán* (trap) refers to a fish trap; *tí* (foot) refers to a snare for catching rabbits. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written as *dí*.
Regarding the "three" mentioned below, there is one type consisting of two hundred thousand *ślokas*. There are four kinds of *ślokas*: the first is named *anuṣṭubh-śloka*;
this does not depend on whether it is prose or verse, but if the number of syllables reaches thirty-two, it constitutes one.
1. *Gāthā* (one verse): This is called *fěngsòng* (recited verse) or *zhísòng* (direct verse), meaning that the Dharma is taught in verse rather than as prose.

The old translation is "isolated verse" (*gūqǐ*). 2. *Geya* (three names): This is called *yìngsòng* (corresponding verse). The old translation is "repeated verse" (*chóngsòng*). 3. *Geyān* (four names):
This is called *jíshī sòng* (collective-bestowing verse). It means to collect many meanings and bestow them through a few words. The old translation is "verse of collected giving."
He recited it; what is now called the "Two Hundred Thousand Verses" is likely the *Anuttara-sūtra*.
As for the fourteen lines, ancient scriptures took seventeen characters as one line.

Later generations corrupted the established system, sometimes increasing or decreasing the count—neither more nor less—because the True Emptiness realized therein has neither expansion nor contraction.

Second, the following section clarifies that the extensive and abbreviated teachings, etc., are equal; this means that not only is the referent (*abhidheya*)—the One Reality—the same, but even with respect to the designator (*abhidhāna*), their meaning is equal.

Therefore, one must not give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority regarding the two teachings, the extensive and the abbreviated. The text is divided into three parts: first, the simultaneous designation of both through the Dharma using the term "perfect sound" (*samyagghoṣa*);
fourth, the explanation of "elegant admonitions" (*yagaok*) as being both extensive and abbreviated. "Elegant" (*ya*) means correct; "admonition" (*gaok*) means awakening.

By means of extensive and abbreviated teachings, sentient beings are awakened and led back to the Right Path. Thus it is said: "Mutually encompassing" (*xiāngshè*). "Viewing" (*shì*) refers to the differing requirements:

for those who are dull-witted, the extensive [teachings] are appropriate; for those who are sharp-witted, the abbreviated [teachings] are appropriate. In reality, when this abbreviated version is presented below, it merely points to the fundamental root;
whereas that extensive version fully discusses the branches and details. Both speak of the same tree; therefore, they are said to be mutually inclusive.
Second, as for "he then [proceeds]," this raises an analogy to provide a dual explanation. Regarding the phrase "hair, mesh, main cord, and collar":
"hair" refers to the nap of a garment; "mesh" refers to the openings in a net; "main cord" refers to the strings of the net; and "collar" refers to the collar of a garment.
As for "hair," in antiquity people made garments from animal skins, such as fox-furs or lamb-skins; therefore, it is mentioned below.
The double explanation in six hundred fascicles is a detailed exposition like the listing of individual hairs; the fourteen-line summary is a concise exposition like grasping the main ropes.
Both discuss the "net of robes," so the listing of the hairs is not intended to be tedious, nor is the grasping of the main ropes intended to be insufficient.
"Three and two paths" (sān'èr tú): the "paths" (tú) below refer to the same as "double-knotting.

Regarding the two paths—meaning that the extensive and the abbreviated are equivalent—it is because that extensive discourse merely provides a detailed exposition of the dharmas of the three categories of causes and conditions and the four truths of object and wisdom found in this sutra.

Thus, although the text is extensive or abbreviated, the meaning is equal. The pronunciation of "tú" is *tú*; it is synonymous with "tú-tú" (road/path). In the *Lìjì* (Book of Rites), it is written as "tú."
The character *lè* (埒) means "equal to" or "on a par with. The *Shiji* by Sima Qian states that the Marquis of Wu was so wealthy that his riches equaled those of the Son of Heaven.
Regarding the phrase "one flavor is the same as returning to maturity": "one flavor" (*yī wèi*) likewise refers to returning to the single flavor of true emptiness (*zhēn kōng*).

The second section, "Specific Praise for the Present Sūtra," is divided into two parts. First, the formal praise; second, the specific praise. Within the first part, there are four sections: the first two lines praise the function (*yòng*);
the next two lines praise the essence (*zōng*); and the final four lines praise the substance (*tǐ*). Because attachment is eliminated, one knows that the fruition is accomplished;
because the fruition is accomplished, the principle of emptiness is revealed—this is the sequence. "Washing away the multitude of doubts" refers to the non-Buddhists (*bāiwài*).
Regarding the various views, the three teachings, and the ordinary and sage stages—whether mundane or supramundane—once the characteristic of emptiness is realized, all delusions are swept away.

That which opens up and rescues the correct principle is the Middle Way of True Emptiness; this is what is called the "Correct Principle" (Zhengli) division. Since this division already encompasses both [the Provisional and the True], it partially penetrates the True and the Mere Middle.

Now, speaking according to its primary intent and for those of sharp faculties, the Correct Principle refers exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). How could it merely be praised as being inferior?

The school [of thought] also [teaches that], because of perfect illumination, one is able to see and know—"yi" (抑) is a particle used for emphasis. Because delusion is non-dual, it is termed "sentient beings";
because awakening is non-dual, it is termed "Buddha. Although delusion and awakening differ, the principle of non-duality is the same; "having no head" is an expression of praise for the essence.
Since the principle of perfect emptiness has neither beginning nor end, one cannot see its head when approaching it, nor can one see its tail when following it.

How could this later be grasped through the biased and narrow thoughts and discursive speech of ordinary beings? It is profound and deep; "zhèn" (朕) is pronounced as *zhí* (直), and "yǎo" (杳) is pronounced as *yǎo* (迢).

Regarding the two types of suffering, the sutra text below cites the passage praising the emptiness of suffering and calamity—because it is empty, there is nothing to be delivered—and the emptiness of Bodhi—because it is empty, there is nothing to be attained.

The passage from the Sūtra stating that "one who crosses over all suffering and calamity attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" implies that what is called "crossing over" is actually nameless crossing, and what is called "attaining" is actually nameless attainment.
Second, the concluding praise regarding the "returning to the source" and so forth refers to the path back to one's original nature. [This is established] by means of fourteen lines.
Regarding the summary of those six hundred [verses] as not being essential: how so? The preceding section speaks of "bravery," which is a metaphor for the supreme victory in shattering delusion.
The upper part praises the generation of good, while the lower part praises the eradication of evil.

Second, from "dare" onwards, is the preface to the principles followed in composing this commentary. First, it indicates the principles followed: "to follow" means to adhere to. "Taiya" refers to a mountain.

It is also called Tiantai because it corresponds to the Tai star; thus, "Tiantai" refers to the place where Zhiyi resided. As for Nāgārjuna, he was the thirteenth patriarch of the *Dharmakośa* (Succession of the Dharma).
Because more than a century had passed since the Buddha’s passing, the paths of study had diverged and various schools had become deceptive and confused;
therefore, Nāgārjuna composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to comment on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, clarifying the meaning of the Great Middle Way. This is its name.
The Dharma-nature school (Faxingzong) subsequently spread its teachings to this land during the Later Qin era. Based on the treatise, Huiwen of the Northern Qi established his contemplative practice;
he orally transmitted it to Nanyue, who in turn passed it to Zhiyi. Consequently, the study of the Three Contemplations (sanguan) flourished throughout China.
Thus, all the dharma-gates taught by Zhiyi are merely the unfolding of the principles of Nāgārjuna. To "elucidate" (fahui) means to develop and expand [upon them].
This disperses the profound principles and essential passages of this sutra.
Second, "shu" (庶) and below clarify the benefit of sentient beings; "shu" means fortunate, "yi" (詒) means to bequeath, and "jue" (厥) means "that which.

This refers to bequeathing to future generations of Dharma sons and Dharma grandsons the virtuous plans for cultivating the Way. "Bi" (俾) means to cause; "shi" (室) refers to the mind; "bai" (白) refers to the Way; and "xin" (心) refers to the heart.
"Empty" (*xu*) refers to embodying the Way; the preceding phrase is from the *Mao Shi* and the following phrase is from the *Zhuangzi*, serving as a connective particle.

"The five aggregates are all empty" means that what is fundamentally only emptiness is deluded into becoming the five aggregates; just as one with an eye disease sees flowers in the sky, yet neither the flowers nor the sky possess two distinct characteristics.

This distinguishes [the teaching] from the partial and shallow views of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles, and the specific contemplation of emptiness in the *Bie* (Distinct) vehicle.

In sequence, these three [levels] are specifically described as being "shallow" because they do not accord with the fundamental nature; this refers to the meaning of inferior wisdom merging with its object.

This applies to all five [stages]. Since these are discussed in terms of breaking through death, they pertain to the ultimate similarity [of the stages]; however, they only break through the *pariccheda* (segmented) death and cannot be called "crossing over all suffering.
Nevertheless, the meaning of "crossing over suffering" also applies to all five, including the stage of names and words (*nāma-pada*), which involves intellectual understanding.
The two deaths are fundamentally non-existent within the one mind; is this not the deliverance of all beings?

The "two deaths" refer to the death of limited segments (*bhavāntara-paraṃparā*) within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃsāra*), and the death of transformation (*pariṇāma-nirvāṇa*) outside that realm. The "Golden Mouth" refers to what is proclaimed by the golden-colored body and the karma of speech.
The "four gates" are alternative names for the principle of reality—emptiness, existence, both, and neither—just as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The *Dharmadhātu-samatā* is named the "Great Chapter on Liberation," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is named the "Mother of Buddhas," the *Nirvāṇa* is named "Buddha-nature," and this present sutra is named "Emptiness of the Aggregates.

All of these invoke the principle that is beyond names. Those who primarily dwell in the Gate of Emptiness do so because, although there are four gates, they reside precisely within the gate of emptiness.

Question: What scriptural passage clarifies these four gates? Answer: Form is... [not... *(Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "色不" (form is not...), indicating the original document was incomplete. The translation reflects the available portion.)*

"Emptiness is not different from form" is the gate of emptiness; "form is not different from emptiness" is the gate of existence. "Form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form" is the gate of both together;

"neither form nor emptiness" is the gate of neither. Thus, "it is emptiness and it is form" refers to both together; "form obstructs emptiness and emptiness obstructs form" refers to the negation of both.
Because this is precisely for the purpose of discussing emptiness to sweep away attachments, it is said that the *Prajñāpāramitā* mostly dwells in the gate of emptiness.
Regarding the non-translation of *prajñā*, it is due to its secrecy, its multiple meanings, and because it accords with ancient usage and generates wholesome roots;
thus it was not translated. Master Xuanzang established five principles for this: although *prajñā* could have been translated, it was retained in its Sanskrit form to generate wholesome roots.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Prajñā is weighty and honorable, whereas wisdom (*hui*) is light and thin; one must not substitute the light for the weighty. Furthermore, that there are three types [of *prajñā*] is based on the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* [sūtras].

If one discusses the five kinds of *prajñā*, as in the present text: first, the *prajñā* associated with the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is also called the "companion of *prajñā*," meaning that which is associated with wisdom;
at the same time, both the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are termed *prajñā*. Fifth, the *prajñā* of retinue is also called the "object of *prajñā*";
that is, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) occurring simultaneously with wisdom that can serve as the retinue for *prajñā*.

Therefore, these two are subsumed within the contemplation of the Middle Way. In this school’s doctrinal system, those that are many are condensed into three, while those that are few are expanded into three, so that the triad and the unity mutually integrate and return to the single mind. Thus, "this shore of birth and death" refers to the four [realms] such as Principle;
the "middle stream of afflictions" refers to the forty-one stages of partial realization where ignorance is not yet exhausted; and "the other shore of Nirvana" refers to the ultimate fruition.
The "wondrous enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is the ultimate [fruit], yet one should also take the stage of partial realization (*bhūta-tathatā*) as the "other shore" (*pāra*);

only by maintaining both perspectives can the intent of the sutra be fully exhausted. As for the term "fangcun" (the square inch), secular texts describe it as the human heart-organ, precisely one inch square.

However, the *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that the mind is like a lotus flower opening and closing, and the *Tiewei jing* states that the mind is like a sovereign; these all refer to the physical heart-mass.

Question: The Sūtra states, "By relying on Prajñā, the mind is without hindrance. This explains the mind in terms of the Dharma, which is very convenient; why then is it explained by means of a metaphor? Answer:

When explaining in terms of the Dharma, the meaning is universal, whether broad or concise; this remains the same. When explaining by means of a metaphor, the meaning is specific, being restricted to the concise text.
The concise is direct while the broad is indirect; reflect upon this and it will be understood. The instruction on the Dharma and the instruction on constancy each contain both teaching and practice.
"Principle" has three meanings; "teaching," "practice," and "principle" are all that which may be taken as a model and all that is unchanging. Regarding "all worthy sages and saints" and so forth:

the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is one, yet the understanding of the worthy is shallow while the realization of the sage is deep; thus, there are distinctions. As for "Prajñā is a single dharma": this refers to the Prajñā of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
[The reason for] questioning below is that one fears the term "all is empty" might be confused with the partial or small vehicles; therefore, it is necessary [to clarify].

In the analysis of the text, there are first brief distinctions regarding the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), followed by distinctions regarding the universal and the specific. Regarding the "complete dharma" possessed by the mundane:

this refers to the original presence of the three thousand realms within each of the ten realms. Regarding "the Middle as immovable," Jingxi states that the nature of the mind is immovable, and the name "Middle" is provisionally established for it.
Regarding "distant and near, skillful and unskillful," the ten realms are "distant" while the six realms are "near"; these refer to the analytical [teachings] of the *āgamas*.
The "emptiness that penetrates" refers to skill and clumsiness within the realm of emptiness (*ākāśa-dhātu*). The distinction between gradual and sudden refers to skill and clumsiness outside of it.
Regarding the three preceding [vehicles], they do not possess the complete dharma; only the Perfect [Vehicle] possesses it. Speaking in terms of both granting and withholding:

to grant it the designation of "emptiness of persons" while withholding the name of "dharma-emptiness" constitutes a partial grant and a partial withholding. If it were withheld entirely, then even the "Supreme" would be non-existent.

Because one undergoes the birth and death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), giving [the teaching] in its entirety ensures that all [afflictions] are eliminated; because the provisional and the real of the birth and death of fragmentation (*bheda-jarāmaraṇa*) have been shattered, it is precisely through emptiness (*śūnyatā*) that attachments are destroyed.
Now, the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) are perfectly interfused and are never otherwise; yet, in accordance with the capacities of beings, there are differences in how diseases are treated.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*): though it possesses a precious, brilliant, and perfect body that is eternally without a single flaw, when shown to people, some may say:
Regarding its brilliance, some speak of its roundness, while others speak of its possession of jewels. The *Prajñā* treatises discuss emptiness to point toward its non-existence;
how could the essential substance of the "jewel of the mind" fail to be precious and perfect? Since ancient times, human teachers have failed to recognize this great principle:

some claim that Prajñā is a teaching of formlessness (*animitta*), some call it the school of total cessation and non-reliance, and some label it the school of deceptive appearances and unreality, asserting it to be inferior to the *Avataṃsaka*.
The principle of *nirvāṇa* is still inferior; those who cling to the polished [teachings] as being the true pearl do not realize its worth.

Now, by speaking of the peripheral and the orthodox, one may understand for oneself that when we examine the various schools' doctrines regarding their mutual inclusion and reconciliation, their relative superiority and inferiority become distinct.

Yet, the perfect principle is fundamentally the same, and the King of Sutras is without distinction. From the Bodhisattvas downward, the realization of the ultimate essence is clearly manifest and possesses its own limits.

Therefore, there are two fruits. As the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "The Bodhisattva relies on Prajñā," and so forth, up to "ultimate Nirvāṇa," which refers to the fruit of realization (*pratisamvid-phala*).
The Sūtra also says, "The Buddhas of the three periods rely on Prajñā and thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," which refers to the ultimate fruit (*atyanta-phala*).
Regarding the four functions: delivering [beings] across the two deaths is the function of destroying evil; attaining the two fruits is the function of generating goodness.
Regarding the "use" and "measure," there are two deaths and two fruits attained; these both pertain to the fruit of the ultimate wisdom of Bodhi and the fruit of the cessation of Nirvana.
As for the "lower teaching" among the five teachings, it refers to the words spoken by the Sage for those below him; "teaching" means providing a model, enabling people to emulate it.
"Matured butter" (susa) follows the analogy of the five flavors in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*; thus, the *Avataṃsaka* is like milk, while the Deer Park [teachings] are like...
Curd is like fresh butter (*navanīta*); Prajñāpāramitā is like matured butter; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras are like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
This is stated according to the sequence of adapting to the capacities of sentient beings, and does not discuss the relative density or thinness of the essence of the Dharma itself.

Dharmakīrti was a person from Kaśmīra, and Dharmapāla was a person from the Western Regions; both came to this land during the Tang dynasty. Including these four individuals, they were all validated by the Buddha’s seal and are all named "Buddhas."
Regarding the statement "at Vulture Peak," the version translated by Dharmacandra reads: "At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak within the great city of Rājagṛha.

As for the fact that this sūtra lacks a preface and so forth, commentaries on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* all supplement the text with the words of the commentary to complete the three divisions, which is like cutting off a crane to fit it to a standard length.
[The text] continues: "It is difficult for a wild duck to form a single body; this is a division of the *Bunbun-kyō* (Sūtra on Divisions).
Since the sūtra itself is purely the primary [teaching], what need is there to supplement it? Regarding the "compiler" (*kyōka*), Ānanda is the compiler of the sūtras.

However, these two sections—the first being a record of events by Ānanda and the second being a record of words by Ānanda—show that the compilation did not go beyond words and events. Why, then, does the author of the commentary (*sho*) not [address this]?

If you argue that the *jì* (narrative) constitutes the *xùfēn* (introductory section) and the *yán* (discourse) constitutes the *zhèngshuōfēn* (main explanatory section), what is wrong with this division?

Now, examining the text of the *Shū* (Commentary), it is evident that this meaning is clearly present. The initial statement "marking the commencement" (*biāoqǐ*) refers to the narrative of the commencement;

the subsequent section explicitly states "benefiting others" (*lìtā*), which is the main explanation. Is this not precisely the division of the Sūtra into two sections: the Introduction and the Main Explanation? However, within the Introduction, [it only...]
If this separate introduction and the general introduction are both perfectly polished, why did the commentary previously state that there is no introduction or circulation section?
The answer is: this refers to the translation by Dharmachandra, which indicates that the passage recording the occasion should properly belong to the main body of the teaching;
thus, that sutra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying: 'I wish to [speak] here...'"
Within the assembly, it was said: "I pray that the World-Honored One will listen to what I, a bodhisattva of universal wisdom-treasury, have to say regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a subtle and wondrous voice, addressed Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"O Great Compassionate One, listen to what you have to say; it shall serve as a great illumination for all sentient beings. This constitutes the introductory section.

The Sūtra states: "Thereupon, Avalokiteśvara, having received the Buddha’s permission and being sustained by the Buddha’s mindfulness, entered the samādhi of the Samyak-saṃprajanya of the Buddha’s Wisdom-Light.

Let the practitioner illuminate it, the reader comprehend it, and the expounder demonstrate it. Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Because there are three types of delusion, faculties, and inclinations, the aggregates, bases, and elements are taught. "Delusion" refers to being confused; for the sake of sentient beings whose minds are thus deluded, the Buddha [taught these].
When teaching for those who are deluded regarding form (*rūpa*), one speaks of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which combine form and separate out mind (*citta*).

For those deluded regarding both, one speaks of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), which separate out form and combine mind. Furthermore, for those deluded regarding both mind and form, one speaks of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), in which both mind and form are separated out.

Moreover, these three are taught in accordance with superior, middling, and inferior faculties; furthermore, they are taught as three because some delight in brevity, some in the intermediate, and some in detail. Now, regarding these three:

The meanings of the *dharmas* and so forth have been presented here only in broad outline; there is no need for detailed discussion. I fear that were this scripture to become a mere enumeration of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), it would lose its true spirit and fail to eliminate attachment. Since the primary intent of this text lies precisely in this, the essential points should be distinguished rather than confused.

Therefore, even the Master of the Tripitaka, upon reaching this point, pointed to treatises such as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and this present commentary does likewise, merely providing a brief indication of the number of categories. As for "combining forms into one": [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific list of dharmas.* As for "combining forms into one": [the text explains that] when various material qualities are aggregated, they are designated as a single "form" (*rūpa*). This is because, although the constituent parts differ, their common characteristic of resistance (*sapratighatva*) allows them to be subsumed under a single category. Thus, by synthesizing these diverse elements, one arrives at the conventional designation of "one form. This principle applies analogously to the other aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). By understanding how these are categorized and synthesized, one avoids the error of proliferating conceptual constructs and remains faithful to the sūtra’s intention to transcend all mental fabrications.

Form (*rūpa*) is a phenomenon characterized by resistance; it is called "form-form" (*rūpa-rūpa*). There are fourteen kinds of form, namely: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the five sense faculties (*indriya*), and the five sense objects (*viṣaya*).

Since these fourteen are all phenomena of form, they are said to be "combined. To expand the mind into four [mental aggregates] refers to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Experiencing the object of cognition is feeling; there are six kinds of feeling, which are caused by the six types of contact (*sparśa*).

Since the objects that give rise to the six types of sensation (vedanā) are distinguished as being agreeable, disagreeable, or neither agreeable nor disagreeable, the six sensations likewise each possess the distinctions of painful sensation, pleasant sensation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation. That which grasps the characteristics of the perceived objects is called "perception" (saṃjñā).
There are six kinds of perception; that is, grasping the characteristics of the six sensory objects (viṣaya) that are experienced constitutes the six perceptions. Thus it is said.

The mental activity that can give rise to a result is called "volition" (*saṃskāra*). There are six kinds of volition, which the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* explains as the "six types of intention" (*ṣaḍ-cetanā*).
Intention is itself karma; it refers to the arising of unwholesome karma, wholesome karma, or immovable karma following each of the six perceptions (*saṃjñā*).
That which discriminates the objects of perception is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). There are six kinds of consciousness, namely the six consciousnesses.

If one were to follow the many masters of the Abhidharma, they would say that consciousness precedes the three [other] mental aggregates; however, all Mahāyāna sūtras clarify that consciousness is always placed last.
Therefore, we shall follow the sequence according to the sūtras.

As for the twelve bases (*āyatana*), "base" (*āyatana*) has the meaning of "growing place" or "source of arising. This means that the six internal faculties (*indriya*) are able to give rise to the six consciousnesses, while the external...
The six objects can draw forth the arising of the six consciousnesses; what was formerly called the "twelve bases" (*dvādaśāyatana*) takes "entering" as its meaning.

When the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) encounter one another, consciousness arises. Consciousness relies upon the faculties and objects, which thus remain the "entrants," while the faculties and objects are themselves the "entered.

The term "twelve bases" is named after that which is entered. Including the mind (*manas*) makes fifteen; this is because the [six] bases are established by opening up the mind from within the aggregates (*skandha*).
This is called "unification" (*ekībhāva*): when the mind-base (*manāyatana*) confronts all phenomena, it possesses the functional capacity to cognize them, and is thus termed "mind.
This "mind" is the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*). Within this context, excluding the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), one takes only the sovereign mind as the mind-base;
therefore, the subsequent explanation states: "The mind-base is taken in its entirety. "Half" refers to one portion of the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*), namely the mental factors. One.
All phenomena that are objects known by the mind are called the *dharmāyatana*. There are two categories that encompass all phenomena:
first, mental phenomena (*caitasika*), which, excluding the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), consist only of the associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*);

second, non-mental phenomena, which comprise past and future form (*rūpa*), the formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Now, excluding those that are not mental factors (*citta-dharma*), the subsequent explanation states: "And a portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). The five faculties (*indriya*) refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five objects (*viṣaya*) refer to form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility. Regarding the physical parts, the location capable of seeing form is called the "eye.
The eye is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*); its substance is formed by the ten types of material form, namely the four great elements.

The four subtle elements are the subtle element of the body-faculty and the subtle element of the eye-faculty. That part of the body which, when facing sound, is capable of hearing sound is called the ear;

the ear is derived matter produced from the four great elements and is composed of ten types of matter, namely, the four great elements, the four subtle elements, the subtle element of the body-faculty, and the subtle element of the ear-faculty.
That part of the body which, when facing fragrance, is capable of smelling fragrance is called the nose; the nose is derived matter produced from the four great elements.

Furthermore, the ten types of matter together constitute the four great elements and the four subtle particles (*anu*). The body-faculty (*kāyendriya-anu*) and the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya-anu*) are the locations capable of cognizing taste when encountering flavor;

this is called the tongue. The tongue is derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced from the four great elements and is also composed of the ten types of matter—the four great elements and the four subtle particles.
It is a composite entity formed by the six parts of the body-faculty and the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya-anu*), capable of perceiving touch when encountering contact.
The locus of touch is all called the body (*kāya*). This body is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), consisting of nine types of matter:
the four great elements, the four subtle particles (*anu*), and the subtle particle of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-anu*); these constitute the five faculties.
Regarding the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*): all forms perceived by the eye are termed "form" (*rūpa*). There are two types of form that encompass all forms:
first, visible forms as primary retribution (*vipāka*), which are the bodily forms of sentient beings, such as blue, yellow, red, white, and black;
second, visible forms as secondary retribution (*niśraya*), which are external objects known as blue, yellow, red, white, and black. All [sounds] perceived by the ear...
That which is heard by the nose is called odor (*gandha*). There are two kinds of odor that encompass all odors:

first, odor arising from the matter of the primary retribution (*vipākaja-rūpa*), namely the vocal sounds and languages of sentient beings; second, odor arising from the matter of the secondary environment (*upādāya-rūpa*).
All matter perceived by the nose is termed odor. There are two kinds of odor that encompass all odors: [the first is as described above]; the second encompasses all external, insentient matter.

First, the fragrances and odors within the physical body (*janma-kāya*). Second, the fragrances and odors within all insentient matter (*ajñāna-rūpa*) external to the physical body that constitutes the environment (*upabhoga-pratyaya-rūpa*).
All matter perceived by the tongue is called flavor (*rasa*). There are two categories that encompass all flavors:

first, the flavor of the sense-base of the physical body (*janma-kāya-rūpa-āyatana-rasa*), which refers to the six flavors within the bodies of sentient beings; second, the flavor of the environmental base (*upabhoga-pratyaya-rūpa-rasa*).
Among all external insentient forms, there are six kinds of tastes. All forms perceived by the body are called "tangibles" (*spraṣṭavya*).

There are two types of tangibles that encompass all tangibles: first, the tangibles of the primary retribution (*vipāka*) within the bodies of sentient beings, such as cold, warmth, roughness, and smoothness;
second, the tangibles of the secondary environment (*upabhoga*), which consist of all external insentient forms.

Tangibles such as cold and heat are also included among the five objects; that which constitutes a portion of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) refers to those non-mental factors within the sphere of mental objects, as previously noted.
Regarding the eighteen elements (dhātus), these consist of the twelve [bases] plus the six consciousnesses. The term "element" (dhātu) signifies a lineage or seed.

The six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) constitute a single category because they share the same nature as faculties; the six objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣad-vijñāna*) are likewise.

Furthermore, the eye faculty, the eye-consciousness, and visible form constitute one category, and the remaining five [senses] are explained by this analogy. Alternatively, it is said that "realm" (*dhātu*) takes "distinct differentiation" as its meaning;

since these eighteen dharmas each possess a distinct essence, their meanings do not overlap, and thus they are collectively designated as such. As for the opening of both "form" (*rūpa*) and "mind" (*citta*), it is opened [to reveal their specific distinctions].
The form aggregate constitutes ten and a half [elements]; the mind element constitutes seven and a half; and within the dharma-element, one portion consisting of mental factors constitutes a half.
The six sense-faculty elements and the six object-elements are to be distinguished as they were in the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding the six consciousness elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*): when the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) encounter one another, consciousness arises.
Consciousness has the function of discernment as its essential meaning; because it relies upon the organs to discern the objects, these six are collectively termed "consciousness.

As for the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*): when the eye organ encounters the object of form, eye-consciousness arises. At the moment eye-consciousness arises, it discerns the object of form; therefore, it is called "eye[-consciousness]."

The element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*)—namely, the elements of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, and body-consciousness—is explained by analogy with the element of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*). Once the five consciousnesses have arisen, they immediately cease;
the mind (*manas*) constitutes the mind-consciousness. This mind-consciousness arises in succession. When this mind-consciousness arises, it cognizes mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).

If the five consciousnesses can give rise to mind-consciousness, then the preceding five consciousnesses serve as its roots, and the subsequent mind-consciousness is the mind-consciousness itself. This is the mind (*manas*).
When the preceding consciousness ceases and the subsequent mental consciousness arises in succession, it is as if the former consciousness gives birth to the latter consciousness.

Thus, the names "root" (*indriya*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are also explained in terms of transmission: that which can produce is called the "root," and that which is produced is called "consciousness.

What is now described as the "mental consciousness element" (*manovijñānadhātu*) refers to this produced consciousness. In this way, the three categories [of the five aggregates] do not transcend matter and mind; matter is entirely created by the mind.
The essence is mind; one should know that all various phenomena arise solely through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Once it is realized that objects are nothing but mind, one then abandons the appearances of external dust. From this, conceptualization ceases, and one awakens to the equality of true emptiness;
therefore, in this sutra, all such things are said to be "non-existent."

Regarding the twelve [links] up to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*): it refers to the fact that two causes produce five fruits and three causes produce two fruits, such that the cycle of rebirth is inexhaustible;

this is precisely what constitutes an ordinary person. First, ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the past, which are collectively termed ignorance because, in the past, the light of wisdom did not yet exist, and thus all afflictions were able to arise. Second, formations (*saṃskāra*) arise from ignorance.

"Birth-karma" refers to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); because wholesome and unwholesome karma can produce karmic results, they are called "formations. The three consciousnesses arise from these formations;
"defiled mind" refers to the momentary state of discernment at the very instant of initial desire for conception during the union of the parents.
Fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which extends from the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) until the stage prior to the branch of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

In the interim, all these stages are collectively termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). From the moment consciousness (*vijñāna*) enters the womb, one week later it is called *kalala*, which means "impure mixture";
its appearance is like solidified cream. After two weeks, it is called *arbuda*, which means "blister";
its appearance is like a small ulcerous blister. After three weeks, it is called *peśī*, which means "congealed mass"; its appearance is like coagulated blood. After four weeks...
It is called *khanumān* (the "Strong Man"), which here [in Chinese] means "congealing and thickening," because it gradually becomes firm and hard.

At five or seven days, it is called *peśī* (the "Flesh-mass"), which here means "the stage of form," because the various sense organs and the distinct shapes of the four limbs are formed. At six or seven days, it is called the "stage of hair, body-hair, nails, and teeth," because hair begins to grow.
At seven weeks, it is called the "stage of possessing the sense organs" (*indriya-sampanna*), because the five sense organs become complete. This is its name.

Regarding the branch of form (*rūpa-anga*): from the stage of the *kalala* up until the fifth stage, the *praśākhā*, although the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*) and the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) already exist, because the four faculties such as the eye have not yet arisen, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet complete; thus, this period is designated as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
From the *praśākhā* stage onward, when the various faculties such as the eye are all fully developed until the time of emerging from the womb, [it is designated as the branch of the six sense bases].
Before the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness has combined to produce the fruit of contact, all are subsumed under the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),

as the six contacts arise from the encounter of the six faculties with the six objects. Thus, from birth until approximately three or four years of age, although the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness is present,
one is unable to discern the objects of suffering, pleasure, or neutrality, and consequently the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) do not yet arise.
All of these are termed "contact" (*sparśa*). The seventh, "feeling" (*vedanā*), refers to the period from age five or six up to twelve or thirteen;
during this time, one is already able to discern the objects of the three types of feeling, yet has not yet given rise to a mind of lustful desire.

The eighth, "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), refers to the period from age fourteen or fifteen up to eighteen or nineteen; during this time, one greedily desires various excellent and wonderful physical attributes as well as sexual desire and the like.

Although the objects are thus [perceived], because one has not yet been able to pursue them exhaustively, it is not called "grasping" (*upādāna*). The nine types of grasping are therefore [the first] nineteen.

After the twentieth year, as one grows older, craving increases further; though one does not rely on [preserving] body or life and feels no fatigue, the essence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) is the same, differing only in degree of intensity.
The tenth [link], existence (*bhava*), is precisely karma; it arises from the pursuit of various objects and initiates wholesome [actions].

Because evil karma draws forth the fruit of birth within the three realms of existence, the eleventh [link], "birth," refers to the moment immediately following the transition from death that binds the fruit of the next life.
The twelfth, "aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*), refers to the ripening and decay of that future fruit; this constitutes aging and death.

Aging and death then give rise to sorrow, lamentation, weeping, and various forms of grief and suffering, which gather together as manifold afflictions. Alternatively, it is said that they arise from the link of "birth."
The subsequent moment-to-moment transformation is what is termed "aging and death," which does not necessarily mean white hair and wrinkled faces.
One who becomes a sage through the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination is one who correctly contemplates the pure true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

thus, ignorance (*avidyā*) is exhausted, and because ignorance is exhausted, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted, continuing until the entire mass of suffering is exhausted. If one can correctly contemplate the three periods of time in this manner, [the cycle of suffering is brought to an end].

By giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*) through the twelve links of dependent origination, one becomes a *pratyekabuddha*. Now, one realizes that both the ordinary and the sage arise from the mind;
because the mind is like an illusion, all realms of ordinary beings and sages arising from the mind are unreal and thus non-existent.

(The middle ten links are omitted here, namely: volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, and birth. A full discussion should be provided.
Regarding "neither practice nor the exhaustion of practice," and so forth, "weariness with suffering" refers to the fruit of birth and death;

it means contemplating how the eight sufferings oppress and the three marks shift and change, thereby engendering weariness and renunciation. "The abandonment of the origin" refers to afflictions and karma, which are able to summon the fruits of suffering;
since one has grown weary of that suffering, one must necessarily abandon its origin. Regarding "rejoicing in cessation and practicing the path": "cessation" refers to the two types of liberation.

The Path refers to morality, concentration, and wisdom; expanded, it consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. To realize the fruit of cessation, one must necessarily cultivate the causal Path.

As for using the aforementioned "attainment-wisdom" (*prāpti-jñāna*) to sever the fruits [of affliction], it is like water: when the water is clear, the appearance of the pearl manifests of itself; one cannot seek it by stirring the water.

At the end of this, there is no principle of attainment; even that which is ultimately severed is called "Nirvana. As for the term "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara-pudgala*), it is named as such because there is nothing further to be severed.
What is now said regarding "that which is severed" refers to the fact that by severing subtle afflictions with the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one attains ultimate wisdom.
Thus, the final mind of Equal Enlightenment is termed "ultimate severance," while what precedes it constitutes the preceding four sections.
Among the ten realms, that which consists of object and wisdom is the Dharma-realm of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

those who have entered the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*) do so because they flow into it spontaneously without the application of deliberate effort. The three obstructions are retribution, karma, and afflictions (*kleśa*);
the four māras are the aggregates (*skandha*), death, afflictions, and the son of heaven (*devaputra*).
As for "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi), it refers to the simultaneous illumination of both sides; because it illuminates both equally and together, it is called Equal Enlightenment.

Regarding "transforming the ordinary person into a sage," this means transforming one who previously dwelt as an ordinary person into a sage who has attained partial realization. Regarding "transforming the cause into the fruit," this means transforming the causal stage of Equal Enlightenment into the person of ultimate fruition.

As for the term *guoluo* (果臝), Guo Pu stated that *guoluo* refers to the *mínglíng* (螟蛉). (Note: The term *guoluo* corresponds to the scientific name *Vespidae*, specifically the mud dauber wasp, which is known in Chinese as *mínglíng*. This wasp is famous in Buddhist literature for its practice of taking caterpillars (*mínglíng*) into its nest and transforming them into its own offspring.)
The slender-waisted wasp (*diēwēng*) is what is commonly called the *diēwēng*. The *mínglíng* is the mulberry caterpillar.

When the *guǒluǒ* (the mud-dauber wasp) carries the *mínglíng* offspring into a hollow tree, they become its own offspring after seven days. The *Fáyán* states: "When the *mínglíng* offspring has died and encountered a *guǒluǒ*, it prays:
'Be like me! Be like me! After a long time, it resembles them. The commentary notes that *xiào* means "to resemble. Thus, when the *guǒluǒ* encounters [the caterpillar]...
The *mínglíng* (cicada larvae) undergoes transformation over a long period and eventually becomes a bee; "to be slain by calculation" (*yì yú jì*) means to die through stratagem.

The pronunciation of "zhù" is that of *zhòu* (incantation). A poem says: "The *mínglíng* has offspring, and the *guǒluǒ* (dove-cocoons) carries them; you instruct your children, so that they may become good like it.
Master Zheng’s commentary states: "‘Shì’ means ‘to employ’; ‘gǔ’ means ‘good. Today, those who instruct the myriad people through the path of goodness are likewise like this."
The *guǒluǒ* (Cucurbita moschata) is therefore used here as a metaphor for the Buddha, while the *mínglíng* (a kind of caterpillar) is a metaphor for sentient beings.
Regarding the statement that "all are of the nature of *zhòu* (incantations)," if one provides this interpretation, it is not only this sutra that reveals that names are *zhòu*;

rather, one comes to know that throughout the entire dispensation of the One Vehicle, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—according to the Buddha’s fundamental intention—are capable of being called *zhòu*, as they cause all to become like the Buddha. While following the stronger and more correct sense, we provisionally designate the Esoteric [Teachings] as such.

Regarding the statement that it is called a "divine mantra" (*mantra*) because it removes obstacles: "divine" (*deva*) refers to the celestial mind; it removes the three obstacles and reveals the three virtues.

This natural principle is in truth due to *prajñā*, and is therefore called a divine mantra. "The wisdom that reflects without obscurity" means that one thoroughly realizes that ignorance is itself the luminosity of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
"Furthermore, there is no surpassing excellence" means that it transcends the partiality of the Hīnayāna. "It stands alone and peerless" is because it is without fault.
The reason it is uniquely transcendent is that it universally eradicates all signs of attachment, such that no dharma can be used as its equal.
This merely explains the "no equal" in the phrase [from the sutra]; however, the meaning of the subsequent word "equal" (等) remains unclarified. "Four *sīt* (悉)" refers to the four *sītān* (悉檀).
*Sīt* means "universal," while *tān* is translated as "bestowal" (*dāna*). This means that the four [teachings], beginning with joy, are universally bestowed upon sentient beings. As for "that is":

Because the principle is the same yet the phenomena are different, there are six [aspects of] "dark" meditation; those who practice such meditation often possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*), while those who rely on words attribute merit to others.

Both cases arise from not understanding these six [aspects]. Furthermore, regarding the current [teaching], one may horizontally distinguish the six through the four *siddhārtha* (the fourfold purpose), and vertically discuss the five "identities" (*ji*).

Within each of these five identities, the horizontal aspect is fully present, and they can likewise be subsumed under the vertical progression of the four [purposes]. Thus, the first identity is that of "name" (*nāman*).
The joyful contemplation of practice gives rise to the semblance of goodness, which thoroughly penetrates the principle of destroying evil.

That which is called "divine mantra" (*deva-mantra*) is so named because "divine" (*deva*) signifies the unfathomable; by means of wisdom one perceives this unfathomable principle, and thus joy arises. That which is called "luminous mantra" (*vidyā-mantra*) is so named because wisdom illuminates and brings forth goodness.
That which is called "unsurpassed mantra" (*anuttara-mantra*) is so named because wisdom destroys delusion and evil such that nothing further remains.
Because one has transcended [all phenomena], those who enter into principle realize the peerless principle through the wisdom of true emptiness; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

That the peerless principle is such that Buddhas and sentient beings are mutually equal is called "equality with the unequaled" (*asamasama*), for the *dharmakāya* of both is identical. Thus, the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the Buddha-fruit are mutually equal and balanced.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The single body and the single wisdom, as well as the powers and fearlessnesses, are likewise so."
The question below asks "Why? and the answer below demonstrates it by showing that the paths of all Buddhas are equal.
Regarding the phrase "only secretly teaching the mind of ultimate reality," the meaning is already complete by simply stating that he "secretly teaches the mind of non-attainment.

The inclusion of the three characters "prajñā-pāramitā" (般若) seems redundant; even if the text were made explicit, there would be nothing more than what is found in the formal language of the scriptures.
To "know" [this] means it is ordinary and commonplace. For example, the *Da Wu* (Great Martial) ritual uses soft hair to summon oxen and sheep, and clear, purified wine to summon water and spirits;
those of common and vulgar understanding do not realize this, and thus they treat the secret invocations as something different from the actual oxen, sheep, water, and spirits.
Those who understand through such analogies—let the wise contemplate this! As for why there is nothing here that is not taken up [by others], it is because... [the text is incomplete].

Furthermore, to prevent others from offering forced interpretations, I have [recorded] these [points] or separately refuted them, hoping to assist in describing the benefits of this work for both self and others,
so that all may together reach the Way.
*Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra-śāstra-yimou-chao* (End).
